explanations.explanation: Joshua, Israel's leader, says it plainly: “All this time you have not deserted your brothers, up to this very day, but have kept the charge given you by the LORD your God.” That's a long stretch of showing up, friend. Most of us can't keep a plant alive that long, and these three tribes kept their word.

Joshua, Israel's leader, says the opposite. He tells the three tribes, “All this time you have not deserted your brothers, up to this very day, but have kept the charge given you by the LORD your God.” So they stuck around the whole time. It's a nice thing to hear from your leader before the trip home.

explanations.answer: Love the LORD and hold fast to Him
explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. Joshua points them to what Moses, the servant of the LORD, gave them: “…to love the LORD your God, to walk in all His ways, to keep His commandments, to hold fast to Him, and to serve Him with all your heart and with all your soul.” Love and holding on come first in that list. The rest of it flows from there.

explanations.answer: Guard the Jordan and keep the peace
explanations.explanation: The Jordan does come up in Joshua's speech, but only as where their homes are. He says they may return to the land Moses gave them across the Jordan. The law he points to is about the LORD: “…to love the LORD your God, to walk in all His ways, to keep His commandments, to hold fast to Him…” Nothing in there about standing guard at a river.

explanations.answer: Bring their wealth to the tabernacle
explanations.explanation: Wealth does show up in this farewell, but later and in a different way. Joshua tells them to divide the spoil with their brothers. The law he reminds them of is about their hearts: “…to love the LORD your God, to walk in all His ways, to keep His commandments, to hold fast to Him, and to serve Him with all your heart and with all your soul.” It's a heart assignment first.

Joshua says, “Divide with your brothers the spoil of your enemies.” These tribes are going home rich, and he tells them to share it. Think of it like baking a big batch of cookies and not eating the whole tray alone. Okay, I've been tempted.

Selling is a fair guess when you're holding a pile of loot, but Joshua never mentions it. He says, “Divide with your brothers the spoil of your enemies.” The word is divide, so the brothers get a share. Nobody's opening a shop here.

Nothing is going up in flames in this blessing. Joshua says, “Divide with your brothers the spoil of your enemies.” That means sharing, not setting a bonfire. I only burn things by accident, and my oven timer is usually the culprit.

An altar, friend. The Reubenites, the Gadites and the half-tribe of Manasseh build an imposing one at Geliloth, right by the Jordan. The text calls it imposing, so picture something you'd see from far off. Keep an eye on that altar, because it's about to cause a stir.

A tower would be big, and the text does say what they built is imposing. But the verse says they built an altar there by the Jordan. It's the altar that gets everyone talking in the rest of this passage.

No city here. The three tribes are on their way home to Gilead when they stop at Geliloth near the Jordan. The text says they built an imposing altar there. One big altar was enough to get all of Israel's attention.

The report puts the altar somewhere else. It says they built it “on the border of the land of Canaan, at Geliloth near the Jordan on the Israelite side.” That's the Canaan side of the river, not out in Gilead. So the altar sits close to the rest of Israel, which helps explain why the news travels fast.

The report says the altar is “on the border of the land of Canaan, at Geliloth near the Jordan on the Israelite side.” So it isn't out in Gilead on the far side. It's on the Canaan side of the river. The details of where it sits are part of the report Israel hears.

Yes, war. When they heard the report, the whole congregation of Israel assembled at Shiloh to go to war against the three tribes. That's a big jump from hearing about one altar. I think they were very worried about what it meant.

No blessings at this meeting. The report lands, and the whole congregation assembles at Shiloh to go to war against the three tribes. A blessing does come later in this story, but from a different moment.

Sharing the spoil was Joshua's instruction when he sent the three tribes home. This gathering at Shiloh is a different scene. After hearing about the altar, the whole congregation assembles to go to war against them. Nobody is passing out anything at this meeting.

explanations.answer: One family leader from each tribe
explanations.explanation: That's right. The text says Israel sent ten chiefs, “one family leader from each tribe of Israel, each the head of a family among the clans of Israel.” Phinehas, son of Eleazar the priest, goes with them. It's a delegation from every tribe, so everybody has someone in the room.

Even with war on the table, the text doesn't send soldiers. It sends ten chiefs, “one family leader from each tribe of Israel, each the head of a family among the clans of Israel.” They're family heads from the clans. Phinehas, son of Eleazar the priest, goes along with them.

There's one priest in this group, and it's Phinehas, son of Eleazar the priest. The ten chiefs are described as “one family leader from each tribe of Israel, each the head of a family among the clans of Israel.” So they're clan heads, one from each tribe.

That's how the delegation sees it. They ask, “What is this breach of faith you have committed today against the God of Israel by turning away from the LORD and building for yourselves an altar…” That's a serious charge to bring against your own brothers. I think they came in hot because they were afraid of what the altar meant.

Wealth came up earlier, when Joshua sent the three tribes home with their silver and gold. But the delegation says nothing about showing off. They call the altar a “breach of faith” and ask about “turning away from the LORD.” Their concern is about faithfulness to the LORD.

Land is a big theme in this chapter, but the delegation doesn't accuse them of grabbing any. They say, “What is this breach of faith you have committed today against the God of Israel by turning away from the LORD…” The charge is about the LORD, not about acreage.

The warning is bigger than that. The leaders say, “If you rebel today against the LORD, tomorrow He will be angry with the whole congregation of Israel.” So it isn't only the three tribes who would feel it. They're saying what one group does can touch everybody.

Right. The leaders warn, “If you rebel today against the LORD, tomorrow He will be angry with the whole congregation of Israel.” The whole congregation, not just three tribes. That's why they didn't just shrug and go home.

explanations.answer: Cross over and settle among them
explanations.explanation: That's the offer. The leaders say, “If indeed the land of your inheritance is unclean, then cross over to the land of the LORD’s possession, where the LORD’s tabernacle stands, and take possession of it among us.” They're ready to make room for their brothers. Not a bad offer from people who showed up ready for a fight.

explanations.answer: Build a tabernacle of their own
explanations.explanation: The offer goes the other way. The leaders say to cross over to the land where the LORD’s tabernacle stands. They also say, “…do not rebel against the LORD or against us by building for yourselves an altar other than the altar of the LORD our God.” So building something of their own is exactly what they ask them not to do.

The leaders never mention cleaning the land with offerings. Their offer is that the three tribes “cross over to the land of the LORD’s possession, where the LORD’s tabernacle stands, and take possession of it among us.” It's an invitation to come settle with them.

The leaders say the opposite. About Achan, son of Zerah, they say, “Yet it was not only Achan who perished because of his sin!” His unfaithfulness regarding what was set apart for destruction brought wrath on the whole congregation. They're saying one person's sin reached beyond that person.

Yes. The leaders remind them that Achan, son of Zerah, was unfaithful regarding what was set apart for destruction, bringing wrath on the whole congregation. Then they add, “Yet it was not only Achan who perished because of his sin!” His sin cost others too.

The tribes say, “If this was in rebellion or breach of faith against the LORD, do not spare us today.” Think about that. They're saying that if they're guilty, go ahead and don't go easy on them. That's a bold way to start a defense.

Trust is a fair guess, since trust is what's at stake here. But the tribes say, “If this was in rebellion or breach of faith against the LORD, do not spare us today.” They're saying that if they're guilty, no mercy.

Following isn't what they ask Israel to stop doing. They say, “If this was in rebellion or breach of faith against the LORD, do not spare us today.” That word is spare. They put themselves on the line if the charge is true.

explanations.answer: You have no share in the LORD
explanations.explanation: That's their fear. They say future descendants might tell theirs, “For the LORD has made the Jordan a border between us and you Reubenites and Gadites. You have no share in the LORD!” So the river itself was part of the worry. I think it would sting to hear that, friend.

Desertion is a charge Joshua already put to rest when he said they had not deserted their brothers. The fear they name here is different. They say descendants might tell theirs, “You have no share in the LORD!”

The tribes don't say anyone will claim their land. Their fear is about the LORD, because descendants might tell theirs, “You have no share in the LORD!” They bring up the Jordan as a border between them. It's about belonging to the LORD.

A witness, baker. They say, “…let it be a witness between us and you and the generations to come, that we will worship the LORD in His presence…” Something people can see long after everyone in this conversation is gone. It's a bit like a photo on the fridge, but made of stone.

A warning would point at danger, but the tribes aren't warning anyone. They say, “…let it be a witness between us and you and the generations to come…” It's meant to say something about who they worship.

Nobody's handing over a present here. The tribes say, “…let it be a witness between us and you and the generations to come, that we will worship the LORD in His presence…” The altar stands there to say something to the future.

explanations.answer: A replica of the LORD's altar
explanations.explanation: That's what they'd point to. They say they would answer, “Look at the replica of the altar of the LORD that our fathers made, not for burnt offerings or sacrifices, but as a witness between us and you.” So it's a copy and not a rival. Showing someone a copy would've saved me some explaining back in the drawer.

No scrolls come up here. The tribes say they would answer, “Look at the replica of the altar of the LORD that our fathers made, not for burnt offerings or sacrifices, but as a witness between us and you.” They'd point to something people could stand in front of.

Moses, Israel's earlier leader, did give them their land across the Jordan (Joshua 22:4). But that isn't what they say they'd point to. They say, “Look at the replica of the altar of the LORD that our fathers made, not for burnt offerings or sacrifices, but as a witness between us and you.”

They say the opposite. The tribes say, “Far be it from us to rebel against the LORD and turn away from Him today by building an altar for burnt offerings, grain offerings, or sacrifices, other than the altar of the LORD our God, which stands before His tabernacle.” So the altar for their offerings is the LORD's own, before His tabernacle. The one by the Jordan isn't for that.

Right, friend. They say, “Far be it from us to rebel against the LORD and turn away from Him today by building an altar for burnt offerings, grain offerings, or sacrifices, other than the altar of the LORD our God, which stands before His tabernacle.” Their offerings belong on the LORD's altar. The one they built is a witness and not a second place to sacrifice.

They were. The text says that when Phinehas the priest and the chiefs heard what the descendants of Reuben, Gad and Manasseh had to say, “they were satisfied.” Everybody walked in expecting a fight and left with an answer. I bet those chiefs felt a lot lighter on the walk back.

The text says the opposite. When Phinehas the priest and the chiefs heard what the descendants of Reuben, Gad and Manasseh had to say, “they were satisfied.” So the answer settled the matter. A tense meeting ended quietly.

That's what Phinehas says. He tells them, “Today we know that the LORD is among us, because you have not committed this breach of faith against Him. Consequently, you have delivered the Israelites from the hand of the LORD.” It's a big thing to say to people you showed up ready to argue with. Honest, too.

Enemies come up in Joshua's blessing earlier, but Phinehas says something else. He tells them, “Consequently, you have delivered the Israelites from the hand of the LORD.” That's a different kind of rescue.

No famine in this chapter. Phinehas says, “Today we know that the LORD is among us, because you have not committed this breach of faith against Him. Consequently, you have delivered the Israelites from the hand of the LORD.”

explanations.answer: Bless God and drop the war
explanations.explanation: That's how it ends. The text says, “The Israelites were satisfied with the report, and they blessed God and spoke no more about going to war against them…” They went from gathering for war to blessing God. The whole mood flipped.
They don't march. The text says the Israelites “were satisfied with the report, and they blessed God and spoke no more about going to war against them…” So the war talk stops.

The text never says anyone tears it down. After the report, the Israelites “blessed God and spoke no more about going to war against them…” In the next verse, the Reubenites and Gadites name the altar Witness.
